FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the 
Ceramicware Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 


This standard was first published in 1982. The Committee decided to revise this standard in the light of experienced 
gained during these years. 


Talc, a hydrated magnesium silicate, is one of the most common minerals used in the ceramic industry. It is very soft, 
being used as the standard of No. 1 hardness in Mohr's scale. Mineral masses of the composition 3 MgO.4 SiO,.H,O 
are known as talc, the impure varieties as soapstone and relatively purer massive varieties as steatite. Talc almost 
invariably contains some impurities like carbonates, iron oxide, gangue, etc, which, if present, impart a dark colour 
or produce spots or specks in the ware on firing. 


In ceramic compositions talc provides a cheap source of magnesia, which while acting as a flux also imparts 
properties of high thermal shock resistance, high electrical resistance at elevated temperature, and low dielectric 
loss and low power factor. The latter two being of great significance when currents of high frequency are applied. 
Therefore, talc finds use in the manufacture of low loss electro-ceramic insulators, low expansion cordierite bodies, 
tiles and glazes. 


The composition of the Committee responsible for formulation of this standard is given in Annex H. 


For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, 
observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 
“Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised)”. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off 
value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

1 SCOPE 


This standard prescribes requirements and methods 
of sampling and test for talc suitable for use in 
ceramic insulator industry and pottery industry.

3 TERMINOLOGY 


For the purpose of this standard, the definitions 
given in IS 2781 shall apply. 


4 GRADES 


4.1 There shall be two grades of the material as 
follows: 


a) Grade I — Suitable for ceramic insulator 
industry, and 
b) Grade IT — Suitable for pottery industry. 


5 REQUIREMENTS 
5.1 Description 


The material shall be in the form of white or slightly 
yellowish/creamish powder free from foliated, flaky 
and fibrous crystals and foreign matter, and shall 
consist essentially of hydrated magnesium silicate. 


5.2 Moisture Content 


Unless otherwise agreed to between the purchaser 
and the supplier, talc powder, as received shall 
contain not more than | percent by mass of moisture, 
when determined by the method prescribed in Annex A. 


5.3 Size Grading 


When tested according to the method prescribed in 
Annex B, the grain size distribution of the material 
shall be within the following limits: 


Not less than 99 
percent by mass 


a) Material passing 
through 75-micron 
IS Sieve 


Not less than 80 
percent by mass 


b) Material passing 
through 45-micron 
IS Sieve 


Or any other size as agreed to between the purchaser 
and the supplier. 


5.4 Specific Gravity 


When tested according to the procedure prescribed 
in Annex C the true specific gravity of the material 
shall be between 2.70 and 2.80. 


IS 10429 : 2011 


5.5 Fired Colour 


The material after heat treatment in accordance with 
the method prescribed in Annex D, shall show a 
uniformly white to cream colour. 


5.6 Fusibility 


The fusibility of talc when expressed in terms of small 
Orton Standard Pyrometric Cone shall be within the 
following limits: 


a) Grade I—Cone 18 to 23 (1 522 - 1 605°C) 
b) Grade II— Cone 16 to 18 (1 491 - 1 522°C) 


The determination of fusion point shall be carried 
out in accordance with the method prescribed in 
Annex E. 


5.7 Chemical Composition 


The material shall comply with the requirements of 
chemical composition as given in Table 1 when tested 
in accordance with the methods prescribed in 
Annex F. Reference to the relevant clauses of Annex 
F is given in col 5 of the Table 1.

6 PACKINGAND MARKING 
6.1 Packing 


The material shall be packed in jute bags or as agreed 
to between the purchaser and the supplier. 


6.2 Marking 
The bags shall be marked with the following: 


a) Processor’s name or his recognized trade- 
mark, if any; 

b) Grade of the material and net mass of contents; 
and 


c) Lot number to enable the material to be traced 
from records. 


6.2.1 BIS Certification Marking 
The bags may also be marked with the Standard Mark. 


6.2.1.1 The use of the Standard Mark is governed 
by the provisions of Bureau of Indian Standards 
Act, 1986 and the Rules and Regulations made 
thereunder. The details of conditions under which 
the licence for the use of Standard Mark may be 
granted to manufacturers or producers may be 
obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards. 


7 SAMPLING 
7.1 Laboratory Sample 


For the purpose of testing, a truly representative and 
homogeneous sample is essential. This shall be 
drawn and prepared in accordance with IS 2109. 


7.2 Test Sample 


Grind 5 to 10 g of the laboratory sample so that it 
passes through 75 micron IS Sieve. Dry to a constant 
mass at 105 + 2°C and use it for the purpose of 
chemical analysis. 


IS 10429 : 2011 


ANNEX A 
(Clause 5.2) 
DETERMINATION OF MOISTURE CONTENT 


A-1 PROCEDURE 


A-1.1 Weigh accurately, nearest to 0.01 g, about 20 g 
of the sample in a tared platinum dish and dry at 105 
to 110°C in an air-oven for 30 min. Cool in a desiccator 
and weigh. Repeat heating and cooling till constant 
mass is obtained. 


A-1.2 Calculation 


m; 
a x100 


Moisture content, percent by mass = 


where 


m = mass ofthe sample taken for the test, in g; 
and 


m, = mass of the sample after drying, in g. 


ANNEX B 
(Clause 5.3) 


DETERMINATION OF SIZE GRADING 


B-1 PROCEDURE 


B-1.1 Transfer about 200 g of the sample to a 
porcelain dish, dry to constant mass at 105 to 110°C 
in an air-oven and cool in a desiccator. 


B-1.2 Assemble the 75 micron and 45 micron IS 
sieves, with the former on top and a pan at the 
bottom. Weigh accurately 100 g of the sample, nearest 
to 0.1 g, and place it on the top sieve. Close the nest 
of sieves with a cover and shake the sieves in a sieve 


shaker for at least 15 min. Stop the sieve shaker, 
remove the sieves and weigh the separated fractions 
retained on each sieve, to the nearest 0.1 g. Calculate 
the mass of the material passing through 45 micron 
and 75-micron IS sieves and express the results as 
percentages of the mass of the sample taken for the 
test. 


B-1.3 Carry out the test in duplicate and report the 
average of the test results on each sieve. 


ANNEX C 
(Clause 5.4) 


DETERMINATION OF TRUE SPECIFIC GRAVITY 


C-1 APPARATUS 
C-1.1 Analytical Balance, accurate up to 0.000 1 g. 


C-1.2 Pyknometer, 50-ml capacity, with a ground 
capillary stopper. 


C-1.3 Vacuum Source, to produce a vacuum of 12 
to 25 mm of mercury. 


C-2 PROCEDURE 


C-2.1 Dry the pyknometer at 105 to 110°C, cool ina 
desiccator and weigh, record the mass as m. Fill the 
pyknometer with distilled water at room temperature 
PC. Insert the stopper and place it in the thermostat 
maintained at a temperature of 2 to 3°C above the 
room temperature. Ensure that temperature variation 
does not exceed 0.3°C at any stage. Wipe the excess 


water from the top in such a manner as not to 
withdraw any water adhering to the outside of the 
pyknometer and weigh recording the mass as m.. 


C-2.2 Empty the pyknometer and dry again at 105 to 
110°C. Introduce about 10 g of the dried sample 
(see B-1.1) and weigh with the stopper in position, 
recording the mass as m,. Remove the stopper, fill 
the pyknometer with distilled water to one-fourth to 
one-half its capacity and boil the water for 15 min 
over a sand bath at atmospheric pressure or under 
reduced pressure, taking care that boiling is not so 
vigorous as to cause loss of sample due to popping. 


NOTES 


1 Where boiling is done at atmospheric pressure, it is 
advisable to insert a thin strip of paper with the stopper 
before the boiling operation. 


IS 10429 : 2011 


2 In place of distilled water, distilled kerosene oil may be 
used in the experiment and in that case formula for 
calculation should be modified accordingly. 


C-2.3 After boiling fill the pyknometer with distilled 
water, cool to room temperature ¢°C in a water bath. 
Insert the stopper, wipe the excess water from the 
top and the outside of the pyknometer as above and 
weigh, recording the mass as m,. 


C-3 CALCULATION 


C-3.1 Calculate the specific gravity as follows: 


(m,-m) 


Specific gravity, £°/t°C 
Ba (m,—m)—(m,—m)) 


where 


t£ = temperature of the water, in °C; 


m = mass of empty stoppered pyknometer, in g; 


m, = mass of stoppered pyknometer filled with 
distilled water, in g; 


m, = mass of stoppered pyknometer and 
sample, in g; and 

m, = mass of stoppered pyknometer with 
sample and distilled water, in g. 


C-3.2 Carry out the test in duplicate and report the 
result nearest to 0.01. The results shall agree to within 
0.03, or additional determinations shall be made in 
duplicate. 


ANNEX D 
(Clause 5.5) 


FIRED COLOUR OF TALC SAMPLE 


D-0 OBJECT OF TEST 


The object of this test is to determine the fired colour 
of a plaque made from the material by heating in a 
suitable furnace at a definite rate of rise of temperature. 


D-1 APPARATUS 


D-1.1 Furnace, of suitable size and capable of 
maintaining a neutral or oxidizing atmosphere. 


D-2 PREPARATION OF TEST PLAQUES 


Take about 200 g of powdered sample. Mix 


thoroughly with sufficient alkali free dextrine, glue 
or starch solution in water and form into test plaques 
in the form of a disc 95 mm dia and 5 mm thick. 


D-3 PROCEDURE 


D-3.1 Carry out heating of the plaques in the furnace 
to 1 260°C in 6 to 8 h. After allowing soaking for 1h at 
the final temperature, shut down the furnace. 


D-3.2 Allow the furnace to cool down to room 
temperature. Take out the fired plaques and note the 
fired colour. 


ANNEX E 
(Clause 5.6) 


DETERMINATION OF FUSIBILITY 


E-0 GENERAL 


The object of this test is to determine the softening 
point of talc by comparing the test cones prepared 
from the material under test with standard pyrometric 
cones heated in a suitable furnace at a definite rate 
of rise of temperature. 


E-1 APPARATUS 


E-1.1 Furnace, A suitable furnace of maintaining a 
natural or oxidizing atmosphere. 


E-2 PREPARATION OF TEST CONES 


Take about 200 g of the dry sample and grind to pass 
through 150-micron IS Sieve, avoiding excessive 


reduction of size. Mix thoroughly with sufficient 
alkali-free dextrin, glue or starch solution in water 
and form into test cones in a metal mould, in the 
shape of tetrahedron measuring 8 mm on the sides of 
the base and 25 mm high. Dry these cones slowly. 


E-3 PROCEDURE 


E-3.1 Mount the test cones along with Orton 
Standard Pyrometric cones covering the appropriate 
range (see 5.6), around the outer edge of a high 
fireclay plaque so that their bases are embedded 
approximately 3 mm deep, and one of the faces is 
inclined towards the centre of the plaque at an angle 
of 82° with the horizontal. 


E-3.2 Carry out heating of the mounted cones, in 
the furnace at a uniform rate of 150°C/h until a 
temperature of 1 000°C is reached. Then reduce this 
rate to 120°C/h and continue heating till the 
deformation takes place. Avoid reducing conditions 
in the furnace during heating operation. Softening 


IS 10429 : 2011 


of the cones is indicated by the top bending over 
and the tip of the cone touching the plaque surface. 


E-3.3 Report fusibility of the material in terms of 
that Orton cone which most nearly corresponds in 
time with complete bending of the test cone. 


ANNEX F 
(Clause 5.7) 


METHODS OF CHEMICAL TESTS FOR TALC 


F-1 SAMPLING AND PREPARATION OF SAMPLE 


The material shall be sampled and prepared for 
chemical analysis as given in 7.1 and 7.2. 


F-2 QUALITY OF REAGENTS 


Unless specified otherwise, pure chemicals and 
distilled water (see IS 1070) shall be used. 


NOTE — “Pure chemicals’ shall mean chemicals that do 
not contain impurities which affect the results of analysis. 


F-3 DETERMINATION OF LOSS ON IGNITION 
F-3.1 Procedure 


Transfer 1g of the test sample to a weighed platinum 
crucible and introduce it in to a muffle furnace and 
slowly raise the temperature to 950 and then to 
1 000°C. After about 30 min, remove the crucible and 
cool in a desiccator and weigh. Repeat the ignition 
and cooling to obtain constant mass. 


F-3.2 Calculation 


m-m, 


Loss on ignition, percent by mass = x 100 


where 


m = mass of the sample taken for the test, in g; 
and 


m, = mass of the sample after ignition, in g. 
F-4 DETERMINATION OF SILICA 
F-4.0 Outline of the Method 


The sample is decomposed by fusion with sodium 
carbonate and extracted with acid. Silica is then 
determined gravimetrically by dehydration and 
baking followed by hydrofluorization. The residual 
silica in the filtrate is determined photometrically 
using molybdenum blue method. 


F-4.1 Reagents 
F-4.1.1 Sodium Carbonate — Anhydrous. 
F-4.1.2 Dilute Hydrochloric Acid —(1:1),(1:3) 


and ( 1 : 19 ) ( v/v) (see IS 265). 
F-4.1.3 Dilute Sulphuric Acid — 1 : | (v/v) (see IS 266). 


F-4.1.4 Hydrofluoric Acid — 40 percent (m/m) 
(see IS 10332). 


F-4.1.5 Potassium Pyrosulphate — Solid. 


F-4.1.6 Ethylene Diamine Tetra Acetate (EDTA) 
Solution — 0.025 M approximately. Dissolve 9.31 g 
of disodium ethylene diamine tetra acetate, dihydrate 
(C,,H,,N, Na,O,, 2 H,O ) in water and dilute to 1 litre. 


10714 2 2~ 8? 


F-4.1.7 Phenolphthalein Solution — Dissolve 1 g 
of phenolphthalein in 100 ml of rectified spirit. 


F-4.1.8 Dilute Ammonia Solution — 1 : 3 (v/v ) 
(see IS 799). 


F-4.1.9 Ferric Ammonium Sulphate Solution — 
Dissolve 40.82 g of ferric ammonium sulphate 
[NH,Fe (SO, ),, 12H,O] in water containing 80 ml of 
dilute hydrochloric acid (1 : 1) and dilute to 500 ml in 
a volumetric flask. 


F-4.1.10 Ammonium Molybdate Solution — 
Dissolve 100 g of ammonium molybdate in water 
containing a few drops of dilute ammonia, filter, if 
necessary, and dilute to | litre. 


F-4.1.11 Oxalic Acid Solution — Dissolve 100 g of 
oxalic acid in water and dilute to 1 litre. 


F-4.1.12 Ascorbic Acid Solution — 10 percent (m/m). 
Dissolve 10 g of the acid in 100 ml of water and filter, 
if necessary. Preserve in an amber coloured bottle. The 
solution, thus preserved, could be used up to 5 days. 


F-4.1.13 Standard Silica Solution — 0.04 mg/ml. 


a) Fuse 0.200 g of pure silica (99.8 percent) in 5 g 
of sodium carbonate in a platinum crucible. 
Dissolve in 300 ml of water, containing 8 to 
10 g of sodium hydroxide, using a polythene 
beaker. Cool and dilute with water in a 
volumetric flask to 500 ml. Store in a polythene 
bottle; and 


IS 10429 : 2011 


b) Prepare immediately before use a standard 
solution containing 0.04 mg/ml by diluting the 
above stock solution appropriately. 


F-4.2 Procedure 
F-4.2.1 Decomposition of the Sample 


Weigh accurately about 0.5 g of the finely ground 
and dried (105°C to 110°C) sample into a platinum 
crucible. Add 3 g of sodium carbonate; after mixing 
intimately, cover the dish with lid and heat over a 
Meker burner, slowly increasing the temperature with 
caution till the mixture fuses. Keep at this temperature 
for 10 min and finally heat till a clear melt is obtained. 
Remove from the burner and cool. Extract the melt in 
a porcelain dish first with water and then with (1 : 1) 
dilute hydrochloric acid. 


F-4.2.1.1 Add about 30 ml of (1 : 1) dilute 
hydrochloric acid and 0.5 ml of dilute sulphuric acid. 
Cover the porcelain dish and allow to stand on a 
steam bath until disintegration of the melt is 
complete. Crush any large flakes with flattened end 
of a glass rod. 


F-4.2.2 Gravimetric Determination of Insoluble 
Silica 

Evaporate the solution in the porcelain dish to 
dryness and allow it to remain on the steam bath for 
another hour. Transfer the dish to an air oven 
maintained between 105°C and 110°C and bake for 
lh. Cool the dish and add 20 ml of (1 : 1) dilute 
hydrochloric acid followed by 30 ml of hot water. Stir 
the mixture till solution of soluble salts appears to 
be completed. Digest the mixture on a steam bath for 
10 min without stirring. Filter through Whatman 
No. 42 filter paper and rinse the dish with (1 : 19) 
dilute hydrochloric acid, scrubbing the basin with a 
rubber-tipped glass rod. Wash the precipitate five 
times with (1 : 19) and hot dilute hydrochloric acid 
and then with hot water until free from chloride. 
Reserve the filtrate and washings for photometric 
determination of residual silica. 


F-4.2.2.1 Transfer both the filter paper and 
precipitate to a tared platinum crucible. Ignite at a 
low temperature until the precipitate is free from 
carbonaceous matter and then heat in the muffle 
furnace at 1 050°C to constant mass (lh being 
normally sufficient). Cool in a desiccator and weigh, 
record the mass as M. Moisten the contents of the 
cold crucible with water, add five drops of dilute 
sulphuric acid and 10 ml of hydrofluoric acid. 
Evaporate to dryness on a hot plate or sand bath, in 
a fume cupboard, taking care to avoid spurting. 


F-4.2.2.2 Heat the crucible and residue, cautiously 
at first, over a gas flame until the disappearance of 
white fumes and finally for 5 min in the furnace at 
1 050°C, cool in a desiccator and weigh, record the 
mass as M, 


NOTE -- If the residue weighs more than 10 mg, repeat 
the treatment with dilute sulphuric acid and hydrofluoric 
acid, ignite, cool, and weigh (as M,). Then fuse any residue 
with 0.5 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate, dissolve in 
10 ml of (1 : 4) dilute hydrochloric acid and transfer 
quantitatively to the filtrate and washings reserved 
in F-4.2.2. 


F-4.2.3 Test Blank Solution 


Prepare a test blank solution using the same 
procedure and quantities of reagents as detailed in 
F-4.2.1 to F-4.2.2.2, but excluding the sample and 
dilute up to 250 ml in a volumetric flask with water. 


F-4.2.4 Photometric Determination of the Residual 
Silica 
Boil the filtrate and washings reserved in F-4.2.2 and 


reduce to about 200 ml. Transfer to a 250 ml 
volumetric flask and make up to the mark with water. 


NOTE — Fusion may, however, be omitted to avoid undue 
attack on platinum crucible. 


F-4.2.4.1 Transfer 10 ml aliquot of the solution 
prepared in F-4.2.4 to a 50 ml volumetric flask. Also 
transfer 10 ml of each of the test blank solution 
prepared in F-4.2.3 to five 50 ml volumetric flasks. 
Add to the five flasks 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 ml respectively 
of the standard silica solution. Then to all the flasks 
add 5 ml of EDTA solution, a drop of phenolphthalein 
solution and then dilute ammonia solution dropwise 
until the colour changes to red. Then add 5 ml of 
ferric ammonium sulphate solution and dilute to about 
30 ml with water (the pH of the solutions should be 
1 to 1.5). 


F-4.2.4.2 Add 5 ml of ammonium molybdate solution 
and allow to stand for 10 min. Then add 5 ml of oxalic 
acid solution followed immediately by 5 ml of ascorbic 
acid solution and dilute the volume to 50 ml. Allow 
the solution to stand for 30 min for development of 
full colour. 


F-4.2.4.3 Starting with the blank ( ‘0’ ml) solution, 
transfer a suitable portion of the coloured solution 
one at a time to an absorption cell, record the 
photometric readings using the light band centred 
approximately at 810 nm. Prepare the calibration curve 
from these readings against concentration of silica 
in mg (as SiO,). 


F-4.2.4.4 Similarly, transfer a suitable aliquot of 
coloured test solution to the absorption cell and note 


the photometric reading for the test solution. 
Convert it to milligrams of silica by means of the 
calibration curve and calculate the silica content, in 
gram (M,) in 250 ml of solution prepared in F-4.2.4. 


F-4.3 Calculation 


Silica, percent by mass = 


where 

M = mass of sample taken for the test in 
F-4.2.1, in g; 

M = mass of crucible and contents before 
hydrofluoric acid treatment, in g; 

M,=mass of crucible and residue after 
hydrofluoric acid treatment, in g; and 

M,= mass of silica present in 250 ml of solution 
prepared in F-4.2.4, ing. 


F-5 DETERMINATION OF ALUMINA 
F-5.0 Outline of the Method 


Aluminium is separated from the aliquot of solution 
prepared in F-4.2.4 as sodium aluminate by treatment 
with sodium hydroxide and is complexed 
quantitatively with EDTA by boiling with an excess 
of the reagent. The excess EDTA is back titrated with 
standard zinc solution at pH about 5.2 using xylenol 
orange indicator. The aluminium EDTA complex on 
boiling with ammonia fluoride liberates EDTA which 
when titrated with standard zinc solution gives the 
amount of aluminium present in the solution. 


F-5.1 Reagents 


F-5.1.1 Dilute Sulphuric Acid — 1 : 1 (v/v). Add 100 
ml of concentrated sulphuric acid ( rd 1.84 ) cautiously 
with stirring to 100 ml of water and cool. 


F-5.1.2 Hydrofluoric Acid — 40 percent ( m/m ). 


F-5.1.3 Sodium Hydroxide Solution — 10 percent 
(m/m). 


F-5.1.4 Sodium Carbonate — Solid. 
F-5.1.5 Dilute Hydrochloric Acid — 1 : 1 ( v/v). 


F-5.1.6 EDTA Solution ( 0.01 M ) — Transfer 100 ml 
of the solution prepared in F-4.1.6 to a 250-ml 
volumetric flask and dilute with water up to the mark. 


F-5.1.7 Methyl Orange — Dissolve 0.05 g of methyl 
orange in 100 ml of water. 


F-5.1.8 Dilute Ammonia ( 1 : 5 ) — Dilute 25 ml of 
concentrated ammonia ( rd 0.9 ) to 150 ml. 


F-5.1.9 Acetate Buffer (pH 5.2 )-- Dissolve 21.5 g 
of sodium acetate ( CH,COONa, 3H,O) in 300 ml of 
water containing 2 ml of glacial acetic acid and dilute 
to | litre. 


IS 10429 : 2011 


F-5.1.10 Standard Aluminium Solution -- Weigh 
0.529 g of aluminium metal ( 99.9 percent purity ) into 
a beaker containing 40 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid 
(1:1) and small drops of mercury. Heat the beaker 
over a water bath. Transfer the solution to a 1 000 ml 
volumetric flask and make up to the mark. 1 ml of 
this solution is equivalent to 1.0 mg of alumina 
(as ALO, ). 


NOTE — Mercury will not dissolve and may be removed 
while transferring the solution to 1 000 ml volumetric 
flask. 


F-5.1.11 Standard Zinc Solution ( 0.01 M ) — 
Dissolve 5.484 5 g of zinc acetate [ Zn (CH,COO ),, 
2H,0 Jin 50 ml of water. Add 0.5 ml of glacial acetic 
acid and 25 ml of acetate buffer ( see F-5.1.9 ) and 
dilute to 1 litre in a volumetric flask. Further dilute 
100 ml of this solution to 250 ml in a volumetric flask 
and find out the equivalent AL,O, in g/ml of this 
diluted solution from the procedure given in F-5.2.3, 
taking 20 ml of standard aluminium solution 
(see F-5.1.10 ). 


F-5.1.12 Xylenol Orange Indicator — Dissolve 0.1 
g of xylenol orange in 100 ml of water containing two 
drops of dilute hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 1 ) (see F-5.1.12). 


F-5.1.13 Ammonium Fluoride — Dissolve 20 g of 
ammonium fluoride in 100 ml of water, add 3 drops of 
xylenol orange (see F-5.1.12) and then dilute 
hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 9 ) dropwise till the colour 
changes to yellow. 


F-5.2 Procedure 
F-5.2.1 Solution of the Sample 


Weigh accurately about 2 g of the finely ground test 
sample (see F-1.1) in a platinum dish. Moisten the 
sample with 5 ml of water. Add 3 ml of dilute sulphuric 
acid and 20 ml of hydrofluoric acid and evaporate 
slowly to dryness on the sand bath or hot plate ina 
fume cupboard taking care to avoid spurting. Repeat 
the process with 10 ml of hydrochloric acid. Cool, 
add 2 ml of dilute sulphuric acid and evaporate as 
before. Heat the dry residue cautiously until fumes 
of sulphur trioxide cease. Raise the temperature to 1 
000°C and ignite for 5 min. Cool and fuse the residue 
with 1 g of sodium carbonate and dissolve in 
hydrochloric acid, cool and dilute to 250 ml in a 
volumetric flask. 


F-5.2.2 Transfer 100 ml aliquot of the solution 
prepared in F-5.2.1 to a 500 ml beaker and nearly 
neutralize with sodium hydroxide solution. Add with 
constant stirring another 100 ml of sodium hydroxide 
solution containing | g of sodium carbonate 
dissolved in it. Allow to stand on a warm water bath 
for lh. Finally cool to room temperature, transfer 
quantitatively to a 250 ml volumetric flask and dilute 


IS 10429 : 2011 


up to the mark with water. Mix well and allow to stand 
for few minutes. Filter through a filter paper 
previously washed with sodium hydroxide solution, 
collecting the filtrate in a beaker, rinsing the beaker 
first with a little filtrate. 


NOTE — Sodium carbonate is used for precipitating 
calcium and magnesium alongwith iron and titanium. 


F-5.2.3 Transfer a suitable aliquot from the filtrate 
to a 250 ml conical flask, add two drops of methyl 
orange indicator followed by 1 : 1 dilute hydrochloric 
acid dropwise until the colour changes from yellow 
to red. Add sufficient EDTA solution to provide an 
excess of at least 5 ml over the expected amount of 
alumina ( 1 ml of 0.025 M EDTA= 1.25 mg ALO, 
approximately ). Add dilute ammonia dropwise until 
the colour changes from red to yellow. Add 5 ml of 
acetate buffer and about 25 ml water and heat to 
boiling for 5 min. Cool, add 5 ml of buffer solution 
and titrate with standard zinc solution using 5 to 6 
drops of xylenol orange indicator. The end point is 
indicated by a clear change from yellow to deep 
orange colour. Add 10 ml of ammonium fluoride 
solution and heat to boiling for 5 min and cool. Add 
5 ml of buffer solution and titrate the liberated EDTA 
with standard zinc solution. 


F-5.3 Calculation 


Alumina, percent by mass = x 100 


where 
V =volume of standard zinc solution required 
for the titration of liberated EDTA, in ml; 
F = equivalent Al,O, of standard zinc solution, 
in g/ ml; and 
M = mass of the sample represented by 100 ml 
of solution taken in F-5.2.2, in g. 


F-6 DETERMINATION OF IRON OXIDE 
F-6.0 Outline of the Method 


The orange-red complex produced in acid solution 
of the sample (pH 4 to 6) by the addition of 
o-phenanthroline is determined photometrically at 
approximately 510 nm. 


F-6.1 Reagents 
F-6.1.1 Tartaric Acid Solution — 10 percent (m/v). 


F-6.1.2 Hydroxylamine Hydrochloride Solution — 
Dissolve 1 g of the reagent in water. Transfer the 
solution to a 100 ml volumetric flask, dilute to the 
mark and mix well. 


F-6.1.3 O-Phenanthroline Solution — Dissolve 1 g 
of o-phenanthroline monohydrate in 90 ml of water 
with gentle heating and constant stirring. Cool and 
dilute to 100 ml. 


F-6.1.4 Acetate Buffer — Dissolve 21.5 g of sodium 
acetate (CH,COONa. 3H,O) in 300 ml of water 
containing 2 ml of glacial acetic acid and dilute to 
1 000 ml. 


F-6.1.5 Standard Iron Solution — Dissolve 0.2 g of 
pure iron in concentrated hydrochloric acid. Dilute 
the solution to about 100 ml. Transfer to a 1 000 ml 
volumetric flask, dilute to the mark and mix well. Dilute 
100 ml of this solution to 1 000 ml in a volumetric 
flask. One millilitre of this diluted solution is 
equivalent to 0.02 mg of iron (as Fe). 


F-6.2 Procedure 


Transfer a 5 ml aliquot of the solution prepared 
in F-5.2.1 to a 100 ml volumetric flask. Also transfer 
0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 ml each of the standard iron 
solution to seven separate 100 ml volumetric flasks. 
Then add to each flask 2 ml of tartaric acid solution 
followed by 2 ml of hydroxylamine hydrochloride 
solution. Stir well and add 5 ml of o-phenanthroline 
solution and 10 ml of acetate buffer solution. Allow 
to stand for 15 min and dilute up to the mark with 
water. 


F-6.2.1 Starting with the blank (‘0’ ml) solution 
transfer a suitable portion of the coloured solution, 
one at a time, to an absorption cell; record the 
photometric readings using the light band centred 
approximately at 510 nm and prepare the calibration 
curve from these readings against concentration of 
iron (as Fe). 


F-6.2.2 Similarly transfer a suitable aliquot of the 
coloured test solution to the absorption cell and note 
the photometric reading for the test solution. 
Convert it to milligrams of iron by means of the 
calibration curve and calculate the iron oxide content 
in the aliquot taken in F-6.2. 


F-6.3 Calculation 


Ferric oxide (as Fe,O,), percent by mass 


M 
= x 0.1429 
M 


1 
where 


M = mass of iron (as Fe) found in aliquot, in 
mg; and 

M = mass of the sample represented by the 
aliquot taken in F-6.2, in g. 


F-7 DETERMINATION OF CALCIUM OXIDE 
AND MAGNESIUM OXIDE 


F-7.0 Outline of the Method 


In an aliquot of the sample solution, R,O, group 
elements are marked by triethanolamine, and calcium 
and magnesium are titrated with EDTA solution at pH 


10 using eriochrome black T indicator. In another 
aliquot magnesium is precipitated out at pH 12 in 
presence of triethanolamine and calcium is titrated 
with EDTA using Patton and Reader (P & R) indicator. 
Subtracting the titre value of calcium from that of 
calcium and magnesium, the titre value for magnesium 
is obtained. 


F-7.1 Reagents 

F-7.1.1 Concentrated Nitric Acid — See IS 264. 
F-7.1.2 Perchloric Acid — 70 percent (m/m). 
F-7.1.3 Hydrofluoric Acid — 40 percent (m/m). 


F-7.1.4 Concentrated Hydrochloric Acid — See 
IS 265. 


F-7.1.5 Triethanolamine Solution — 30 percent (v/v). 
Dilute 60 ml of triethanolamine to 200 ml. 


F-7.1.6 Sodium Hydroxide Solution (5N 
approximately) — Dissolve 100 g of sodium 
hydroxide in water, cool and dilute to 500 ml and 
store in a polythene bottle. 


F-7.1.7 Patton and Reader (P & R) Indicator — 
Mix by grinding together 0.1 g of P & R indicator and 
30 g of sodium chloride. About 0.2 g of the mixture is 
required for each titration. 


F-7.1.8 Standard EDTA Solution (0.01 M) — Same 
as in F-5.1.6. Standardize against the standard 
calcium solution (see F-7.1.9) using P & R indicator 
and against the standard magnesium solution 
(see F-7.1.10) using erichrome black T indicator 
(see F-7.1.12). 


F-7.1.9 Standard Calcium Solution — Dissolve 
1.784 8 g of calcium carbonate dried at 150°C ina 
slight excess of hydrochloric acid, boil to expel 
carbon dioxide, cool and dilute to 1 000 ml. One 
millilitre of this solution is equivalent to 1 mg of 
calcium oxide (as CaO). 


F-7.1.10 Standard Magnesium Solution — Wash a 
piece of magnesium in dilute hydrochloric acid to 
remove any oxide film, then with water and dry it 
with ethanol followed by ether. Dissolve 0.603 2 g of 
the metal in a slight excess of dilute hydrochloric 
acid, cool and dilute to 1 000 ml. One millilitre of this 
solution is equivalent to 1 mg of magnesium oxide 
(as MgO). 


F-7.1.11 Ammonia-Ammonium Chloride Buffer 
Solution (pH = 10) — Dissolve 57.5 g of ammonium 
chloride in 250 ml of water, and 570 ml of ammonia 
(RD 0.88) and dilute to 1 litre and mix thoroughly. 


F-7.1.12 Eriochrome Black T Indicator Solution 
— Dissolve 0.4 g of the sodium salt of eriochrome 


IS 10429 : 2011 


black T in a mixture of 20 ml of ethanol and 30 ml of 
triethanolamine. 


F-7.2 Procedure 
F-7.2.0 Solution of the Sample 


Weigh accurately about 1 g of the test sample 
(see F-1.1) in a platinum dish. Add 5 ml of 
concentrated nitric acid, 5 ml of perchloric acid and 
about 10 ml of hydrofluoric acid. Cover the dish with 
a lid. Allow the reaction to proceed for at least 15 
min, then remove the lid and evaporate the mixture 
to dryness on a sand bath in a fume cupboard, taking 
care to avoid spurting. Cool, add 5 ml of perchloric 
acid, rinse the lid and sides of the dish with water 
and again evaporate carefully to dryness. To the 
cool, dry residue, add 2 ml of concentrated 
hydrochloric acid and about 15 ml of water. Digest 
on a steam bath for 10 min, cool, filter if necessary 
and dilute the solution with distilled water to 250 ml 
in a volumetric flask. Store the solution in a polythene 
bottle. 


F-7.2.1 Determination of Calcium Oxide 


Pipette 50 ml of the solution (see F-7.2.0) into a 
250 ml conical flask. Add 10 ml of triethanolamine 
solution, 5 ml of sodium hydroxide solution dropwise 
while shaking the solution, and then add 0.2 g of P& 
R indicator. Titrate immediately with standard EDTA 
solution until the colour changes from pink to blue. 

NOTE — If sharp end-point is not obtained, add 2 ml of 

potasium cyanide (10 percent, m/v) after the addition of 


triethanolamine. 


F-7.2.1.1 Calculation 
Calcium oxide (as CaO), 


F 
percent by mass = x 100 


where 


V = volume of standard EDTA solution 
required for titration, in ml; 


F = CaO equivalent of the standard EDTA 
solution, in g/ ml, and 


M = mass of the sample represented by the 
aliquot taken in F-7.2.1, in g. 


F-7.2.2 Determination of Magnesium Oxide 


Pipette 50 ml of the solution prepared in F-7.2.0 into 
a 250 ml conical flask. Add 10 ml triethanolamine 
solution. Add 15 ml of ammonia-ammonium chloride 
buffer solution. Add 4 to 5 drops of eriochrome black 
T indicator solution and immediately titrate with the 
standard EDTA solution until the colour changes 
from wine red to blue. 


IS 10429 : 2011 


NOTE -- If sharp end-point is not obtained, add 2 ml of 
potasium cyanide (10 percent, m/v) after the addition of 
triethanolamine. 


F-7.2.2.1 Calculation 


Magnesium oxide (as MgO), 


a nk 
percent by mass = = x 100 


where 


V,=volume of standard EDTA solution 
required for titration of total calcium and 
magnesium required in F-7.2.2, in ml; 

V =volume of standard EDTA solution 
required for titration in F-7.2.1, in ml; 

F = MgO equivalent of the standard EDTA 
solution, in g/ ml; and 

M = mass of the sample represented by the 
aliquot taken in F-7.2.2, in g. 


F-8 DETERMINATION OF ALKALIS AS 
POTASSIUM OXIDE AND SODIUM OXIDE 


F-8.0 General 


Sodium and potassium contents are determined with 
the help of a flame emission spectrophotometer by 
measuring the intensity of radiation emitted at 
767 nm by potassium or at 589 nm by sodium. For 
this purpose use may also be made of a filter type 
flame photometer. In both the cases, however, the 
intensity of radiation either at the specified 
wavelength, or through the relevant filter is compared 
with that obtained for simulated standard solutions 
prepared from potassium chloride and sodium 
chloride solutions. 

NOTE -- Water used in preparing standard solutions shall 

be double-distilled so that it does not produce no deflection 

of the galvanometer when the instrument is set for full 


scale deflection for 10 ppm of potassium or 5 ppm of 
sodium concentration. 


F-8.1 Apparatus 


F-8.1.1 Flame Photometer, provided with 
arrangement for monochromatic light or a set of filters 
required for determination of potassium and sodium. 
The photometer comprises essentially a 
galvanometer, a photo cell or tube and a photo- 
multiplier tube. Other accessories are an atomizer- 
burner (or an atomizer and a burner) fed with liquefied 
petroleum gas (LPG) and compressed air (or oxygen, 
acetylene, etc) in such a ratio that combustion of 
gas is complete. 


F-8.1.2 Burette, of 50 ml nominal capacity 
and graduated in 0.1 ml for Class A accuracy 
(see IS 1997). 


F-8.1.3 Volumetric Flasks, two of 1 000 ml, 2 of 250 ml 
and 14 of 100 ml nominal capacity of Class A accuracy 
(see IS 915). 


10 


F-8.2 Reagents 
F-8.2.1 Hydrochloric Acid — 1 : 1 (v/v). 


F-8.2.2 Standard Sodium Solutions — Weigh 
accurately 0.508 4 g of sodium chloride (NaCl), 
previously dried to constant mass at 110 + 2°C. 
Dissolve in water, transfer to a 1 000 ml volumetric 
flask, dilute to the mark with water and mix. 


F-8.2.2.1 Transfer 10 ml of this solution to a 100 ml 
volumetric flask, dilute up to the mark with water and 
mix. This diluted solution contains 200 ppm of sodium 
(as Na). 


F-8.2.2.2 Transfer 25, 20, 15, 10 and 5 ml respectively 
of the standard sodium solution prepared in F-8.2.2.1 
to five 100 ml volumetric flasks. Add 37.5 ml each of 
potassium solution prepared in F-8.2.3 to the five 
flasks, dilute up to the mark with water and mix. These 
solutions contain 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 ppm 
respectively of sodium (as Na). 


F-8.2.3 Standard Potassium Solutions — Weigh 
accurately 0.381 4 g of potassium chloride (KC1), 
previously dried at 110 + 2°C to constant mass, 
Dissolve in water, transfer to a 1 000 ml volumetric 
flask, dilute up to the mark with water and mix. 


F-8.2.3.1 Transfer 10 ml of this solution to a 100 ml 
volumetric flask, dilute up to the mark with water and 
mix. This diluted solution contains 200 ppm of 
potassium (as K). 


F-8.2.3.2 Transfer 35, 30, 25, 20, 15, 10 and 5 ml 
respectively of the standard potassium solution 
prepared in F-8.2.3.1 to seven 100 ml volumetric 
flasks. Add 26.0 ml each of the sodium solution 
prepared in F-8.2.2, to the seven flasks, dilute up to 
the mark with water and mix. One millilitre of these 
solutions is respectively equivalent to 70, 60, 50, 40, 
30, 20 and 10 ppm of potassium (as K). 


F-8.3 Setting-Up the Apparatus 


Switch the instrument on and wait for its stabilization. 
Adjust the slit and wavelengths (767 nm for 
potassium or 589 nm for sodium) or place the filters 
in position as the case may be. 


F-8.3.1 Pour water in the spray cup, open its tap and 
turn the compressed air or oxygen on. Adjust the tap 
and pressure to establish atomization of water in a 
fine spray. Open the gas tap and light the burner. 
Adjust gas, if necessary, to get complete combustion. 
Next switch the photocell on and adjust the indicator 
needle or the indicator light spot, as the case may 
be, to bring it to the ‘zero’ position. 


F-8.3.2 Atomize potassium (70 ppm, see F-8.2.3.2) 
or sodium (50 ppm, see F-8.2.2.2) solutions in place 
of water (see F-8.3.1) and adjust the deflection to 


full scale. Atomize water once again to check the 
indicator needle or light spot rests at “zero”. Ifit shifts 
from “zero” again adjust it to “zero”. Thus when the 
instrument reads “zero” with water and shows full 
scale deflection for 70 ppm K, or 20 ppm Na solution, 
it is ready for use. 


NOTES 


1 Atomization of any solution should always be followed 
by atomization of double-distllled water till the indicator 
comes to zero position. 


2 Do not disturb the setting of the atomizer or burner so 
that rates of flow are constant for a series of 
determinations. 


F-8.4 Procedure 
F-8.4.1 Preparation of the Sample Solution 


Transfer 50 ml of the solution prepared in F-7.2.1 to 
a 500 ml volumetric flask and dilute up to the mark 
with water. 


F-8.4.2 Calibration Graph and Determination 


Without disturbing the setting of the instrument, 
atomize standard potassium (see F-8.2.3.2) or sodium 
(see F-8.2.2.2) solutions of different concentrations 
in an ascending order and plot the readings of the 
indicator against concentrations and draw the graph. 
Next atomize the sample solution reserved in F-8.4.1 
and note the deflection and calculate concentration 
of potassium or sodium as the case may be. 


Example: 


Suppose reading for 70 ppm K solution in 90.0, 
that for 60 ppm K solution is 72.0 and that for 


11 


IS 10429 : 2011 


the sample solution is T (somewhere between 
90.0 and 72.0) 


Similarly, suppose reading for 40 ppm Na 
solution is 80.0, that for 50 ppm Na solution is 
100.0; and that for sample solution is T 
(somewhere between 80.0 and 100.0). 


Then concentration of potassium (C,) in the 
sample solution is expressed as: 


Cac OY (7-72) ppm

F-8.5 Calculation 


a) Alkalis (as K,O), percent by mass = 1 204C,, 
and 


b) Alkalis (as Na,O), percent by mass = 1 348 Cha 


where 
C, = concentration of potassium (as K) in

ANNEXG 
(Clause 5.8.1) 


DETERMINATION OF CERAMIC AND DIELECTRIC PROPERTIES 


G-0 GENERAL 


G-0.1 These properties are to be determined in 
respect of Grade I of the material only. 


G-1 PROCEDURE 


G-1.1 Make about 3 to 5 kg of a standard steatite 
porcelain body of the composition given below: 


Material Percent by Mass 
Talc 82 
China clay ( Grade I) 8 
Barium carbonate 10 


G-1.2 Charge the raw materials according to the 
composition given above in a suitable milling pot 
along with water and porcelain balls ( 1.3 cm to 2.54 
cm dia ) in the ratio charge : balls : water, 1: 1:1. 
Place the pot in a suitable pot mill and allow to run 
for 8 h. 


G-1.3 Preparation of Test Pieces 


G-1.3.1 For determination of ceramic properties, take 
out the body slip in a tray and allow to dry in an air 
oven up to a plastic consistency, cool and mix 
thoroughly. Extrude out test rods 19 mm in diameter 
and 150 mm long through a de-airing pug mill, with a 
vacuum of about 500 mm of mercury. Put shrinkage 
marks on the rods. Allow the test pieces to dry very 
slowly first in air and then in an air oven. 


12 


G-1.3.2 For determination of dielectric properties take 
out the body slip in a tray and allow to dry in an air 
oven at 110°C. Crush and grind the dried material to 
pass through a 250 micron IS sieve and mix with 
5 percent moisture, | percent starch as binder and 
0.5 percent wax as lubricant. Granulate the mixture 
by squeezing through a 1.00 mm IS sieve. Make discs 
measuring 57 mm diameter and 3 mm thickness by 
pressing in a steel die at a pressure of 25.6 MPa. 


G-1.4 Fire the test pieces in an electric furnace with 
one Orton Standard Pyrometric Cone No. 10. Raise 
the temperature at a uniform rate of about 100°C/h 
up to 1 000°C and then at a rate of 60°C/h until the 
cone is fully bent and allow to soak at that 
temperature for 3 h. 


G-1.5 When the furnace is cooled to about 100°C to 
150°C, take out the test pieces and cool in a 
desiccator. 


G-1.6 Test for Ceramic Properties 


Determine the fired shrinkage, fired modules of 
rupture and percent water absorption using test 
pieces prepared in G-1.3.1 according to the method 
prescribed in IS 4589. 


G-1.7 Test for Dielectric Properties 


Determine the loss of tangent value in accordance 
with the methods prescribed in IS 4486. 


IS 10429 : 2011

of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to copyright be 
addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. 


Review of Indian Standards 

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 
‘BIS Catalogue’ and ‘Standards: Monthly Additions’. 

This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No.: CHD 9 (1682).
